title: Backtracking with Pruning: N-Queens
oneLiner: Place one queen per row; in each row try every column that no earlier queen attacks, recurse, then remove the queen and try the next column.
keyTakeaway: Choose the decision order so most constraints hold automatically (one queen per row means rows can never clash), then track what's left in O(1) sets: used columns, used r - c diagonals and used r + c anti-diagonals. A square is safe exactly when its column and both diagonals are free.
explanation:
Place n queens on an n × n chessboard so that no two attack each other: no two share a row, a column or a diagonal. Return how many different arrangements exist. For n = 4 there are 2, for n = 8 there are 92, and for n = 2 or 3 there are none.

Trying every way to put n queens on n² squares is hopeless. The first insight is that each row must hold exactly one queen, so make the decision "which column does the queen in row r go in?" and go row by row. Rows can then never conflict, and the search space drops to at most n choices per row.

The second insight is how to check a square in O(1). Every square on the same "\" diagonal has the same r - c, and every square on the same "/" anti-diagonal has the same r + c. So keep three sets: columns in use, r - c values in use and r + c values in use. Square (r, c) is safe if c, r - c and r + c are all unused.

The backtracking function place(r) does this: if r == n, every row has a queen, so count one solution. Otherwise, for each column c that is safe, add c, r - c and r + c to the sets, call place(r + 1), then remove them again (the backtrack) and try the next column. A row with no safe column simply returns, which prunes that whole branch: the visualization shows the search on a 4 × 4 board hitting two dead ends before finding its first solution.

The running time is roughly O(n!), since row r has at most n - r safe columns, and space is O(n) for the sets and recursion. Common follow-ups: return the boards themselves (keep a queens[r] = c array and build the strings when r == n), and speeding it up with bitmasks instead of sets, where the free squares of a row are ~(cols | diag | antiDiag) and each step peels off the lowest set bit.

The search doesn't stop at the first solution: it backtracks and keeps going. Its mirror image (columns 2, 0, 3, 1) is the only other one, so n = 4 has 2 solutions.

recognitionSignals: Place items on a board or into slots so that no two conflict (queens, Sudoku digits, colouring a map), and count or list the valid arrangements.
The constraints let you reject a partial placement immediately, so you can prune whole branches instead of generating full candidates and checking them.
n is small (usually 15 or less), which signals an exponential search with pruning is expected.
gotchas: Diagonals: r - c identifies a "\" diagonal and r + c a "/" one. r - c can be negative, so if you use arrays instead of sets, offset it by n - 1.
Undo all three marks (column, diagonal, anti-diagonal) after the recursive call. Removing only the column leaves phantom diagonal blocks.
n = 1 has exactly one solution (a single queen). n = 2 and n = 3 have zero, not errors.
confusableWith: Backtracking: Generate All Subsets (this track) explores every branch because every subset is an answer. N-Queens prunes most branches early because most partial boards are already invalid.
Backtracking on a Grid: Word Search (this track) also undoes marks on a grid, but it walks a path between neighbouring cells; here each row is an independent decision.

complexity.note: Row r has at most n - r columns not already blocked, so the search tree has at most n · (n-1) · ... · 1 leaves; pruning makes it much smaller in practice. The column/diagonal sets and the recursion are O(n).

referenceSolutions.python:
def total_n_queens(n):
    cols = set()
    diags = set()       # r - c is constant along a "\" diagonal
    anti_diags = set()  # r + c is constant along a "/" diagonal
    count = 0

    def place(r):
        nonlocal count
        if r == n:
            count += 1
            return
        for c in range(n):
            if c in cols or r - c in diags or r + c in anti_diags:
                continue
            cols.add(c)
            diags.add(r - c)
            anti_diags.add(r + c)
            place(r + 1)
            cols.remove(c)
            diags.remove(r - c)
            anti_diags.remove(r + c)

    place(0)
    return count
